findings.topic: Cadence with FlightAware push alerts (hybrid model, recommended)
findings.detail: AeroAPI alerts fire on flight plan filed, out/off/on/in, cancelled, diverted, plus bundled departure events (gate changes, delays >30 min, airport delays) and bundled arrival events (en-route changes, delays >30 min). Alert config endpoints are $0.000; Push Alert Delivery is $0.020 per delivered alert (4x a $0.005 status poll). ASSUMPTION: ~8 alerts delivered per flight on average (filed, out, off, on, in, plus ~3 change/delay events); 12 for a disrupted flight. Confirmation poll schedule: pre-48h = 1/day via AeroDataBox (AeroAPI /flights/{ident} cannot see >2 days ahead); 48h..3h = every 6h = 8 polls; 3h..boarding = every 30 min = 5; boarding..landing = every 15 min = 15; post-landing = 2 (gate-in confirm, +2h final). AeroAPI billable events per flight = 30 polls + 8 alerts = 38 (max ~42 with 12 alerts). Cost list = 30*0.005 + 8*0.020 = $0.15 + $0.16 = $0.31/flight (worst case 12 alerts: $0.39). Pre-48h on AeroDataBox: 12 daily polls (14-day lead) x 2 units = 24 units/flight (see ADB unit caveat). TARGETS: <= 60 AeroAPI billable events per flight with alerts (alerts counted as 4 poll-equivalents => <= 50 poll-equivalent budget, current design 30 + 8*4 = 62 poll-equivalents, so set hard cap 75 poll-equivalents = $0.375); <= 250 status polls per flight without alerts (design B = 208, C = 193).

findings.topic: Critical constraint: AeroAPI /flights/{ident} future window is ~2 days
findings.detail: OpenAPI spec for GET /flights/{ident}: default window is 'departures starting approximately 11 days in the past' to 'approximately 2 days in the future'; 'Specified start date must be no further than 10 days in the past and 2 days in the future'; max_pages default 1; a result set = 15 records. Consequence: any refresh earlier than T-48h cannot use the $0.005 status endpoint; the only AeroAPI options are GET /schedules/{date_start}/{date_end} at $0.020/result set (future-date window and max span per query NOT verified in this run; from memory it accepts future dates in ~10-day spans, unverified) or the airport scheduled_departures board at $0.005 (airport-wide, one result set per 15 flights, not per flight). This makes pre-48h polling 4x more expensive per poll on AeroAPI and is the technical reason to route all pre-48h refreshes to AeroDataBox and only hand the flight to AeroAPI (and create the alert) at T-48h. ADS-B feeder/Personal tier: up to $5 free/month ($10 for ADS-B feeders) for dev, 10 result sets/minute.

findings.topic: FlightAware AeroAPI pricing (verified 2026-09-19)
findings.detail: Tiers: Personal (no minimum, up to $5 free/month, $10 for ADS-B feeders, 10 result sets/min, no alerts); Standard ($100/month minimum, 5 result sets/second, includes Flight Alerting, historical data, B2C derivative-works rights); Premium ($1,000/month minimum, 100 result sets/second, Foresight predictions, Aireon space-based ADS-B, 99.5% uptime). Per-result-set fees (15 records = 1 result set): GET /flights/{ident} $0.005; /flights/{ident}/canonical $0.001; /flights/{id}/position $0.010; /flights/{id}/track $0.012; /flights/{id}/route $0.010; /flights/search $0.050; /schedules/{date_start}/{date_end} $0.020; /airports/{id}/flights/arrivals|departures|scheduled_departures|scheduled_arrivals $0.005 each; /airports/{id}/flights $0.020; /airports/{id}/delays $0.010; /airports/delays $0.050; /airports/{id}/weather/observations $0.002; /airports/{id}/weather/forecast $0.002; /airports/{id} $0.015; /foresight/flights/{ident} $0.015; /history/flights/{ident} $0.020; /history/flights/{id}/track $0.060; /aircraft/{ident}/owner $0.002; /disruption_counts/... $0.020. Alerts: POST/GET/PUT/DELETE /alerts and /alerts/endpoint $0.000; Push Alert Delivery $0.020 per delivery. Volume discounts (Standard and Premium): first $1,000/month at list, then marginal discounts 30% ($1K-2K), 51% ($2K-4K), 65% ($4K-8K), 76% ($8K-16K), 83% ($16K-32K), 88% ($32K-64K), 94% (>$64K). ASSUMPTION: discounts are marginal (apply to the increment in each band), which is how the page reads ('each incremental level of usage'). Note: a FlightAware forum thread (Nov 2025) reports /flights/{ident} billed at $0.005 when the user expected $0.001; $0.001 is the /canonical endpoint, so $0.005 is the correct planning number. Third-party blogs quote a $200/month Standard minimum; FlightAware's own page says $100 as of this fetch.

findings.topic: AeroDataBox pricing and unit model (verified, with one unverified multiplier)
findings.detail: Direct plans: Starter $19/month, 40,000 units, 5 req/s; Growth $99/month, 400,000 units, 10 req/s; Scale $499/month, 4,000,000 units, 20 req/s; Custom above that. Overages on direct plans only via ADS-B feeding (no paid overage). Marketplace: Basic free 400 units 1 req/s; Pro $7.50 (API.Market) / $8 (RapidAPI) 5,000 units; Ultra $37.50 / $40 50,000 units 3-4 req/s; Mega $187.50 / $200 500,000 units 5-8 req/s, overage $0.00037-0.0004/unit. Effective unit price: Starter $0.000475, Growth $0.0002475, Scale $0.000125, Mega overage $0.0004. Units per request depend on endpoint Tier (1-4). Verified via search snippet only: Tier 1 = 1 unit, Tier 3 = 6 units, Tier 4 = 60 units; flight status with flight plan returned is charged x2. UNVERIFIED (from memory): Tier 2 = 2 units and the single-day Flight Status endpoint is Tier 2 (the flight-history announcement says the multi-day history endpoint is 'unlike single-day Flight Status API ... placed under Tier 3', so single-day status is below Tier 3). Verified tiers: FIDS (airport departures/arrivals) = Tier 2; flight delay statistics by flight number = Tier 3; airport delay index = Tier 3. Flight History & Schedule endpoint date range per request: 7 days (Basic/Pro), 14 days (Ultra), 30 days (Mega). Flight Alert API (2026): webhook push, subscriptions per flight number or airport ICAO never expire, cost 1 credit per flight item per notification, 1 credit = 1 API unit, you pay proportionally to notifications sent (including retries). Planning number used: 2 units per status poll; sensitivity: if it is 1 unit, halve ADB cost; if 6 units, triple it.

findings.topic: Provider cost per flight by scenario (list price, before AeroAPI volume discount)
findings.detail: S1 'AeroAPI-only polling, cadence B (6h in 7d..48h)': pre-48h 27 polls via /schedules @ $0.020 = $0.54; inside 48h 181 polls (45+14+110+12) @ $0.005 = $0.905; total $1.445/flight. Cadence A would be 127 x 0.020 + 0.905 = $3.45/flight (do not do this). S1-C (daily pre-48h): 12 x 0.020 + 0.905 = $1.145. S2 'Hybrid: AeroDataBox pre-48h + AeroAPI alerts + sparse confirm inside 48h' (recommended): AeroAPI 30 polls x $0.005 + 8 alerts x $0.020 = $0.31/flight; ADB 12 polls x 2 units = 24 units = $0.003 (Scale) to $0.011 (Starter). S3 'AeroDataBox-only polling, cadence B' (dev/secondary): 208 polls x 2 units = 416 units/flight = $0.052 (Scale) / $0.103 (Growth) / $0.198 (Starter); with cadence C: 386 units. S4 'AeroDataBox alerts + sparse ADB polls' (cheapest, data-quality unknown for US gates/inbound aircraft): ~15 notification credits + ~20 polls x 2 units = ~55 units/flight = $0.007 (Scale). Positions (map while airborne): ADS-B community every 30 s for 180 min = 360 polls/flight (180 at 60 s), $0 but rate-limited; AeroAPI /flights/{id}/position would be 180 x $0.010 = $1.80/flight at 60 s, 6x the status cost, rejected.

findings.topic: AeroAPI monthly spend with marginal volume discounts
findings.detail: Discount function (marginal bands): D(L) for list spend L = min(L,1000) + 0.70*clamp(L-1000,0,1000) + 0.49*clamp(L-2000,0,2000) + 0.35*clamp(L-4000,0,4000) + 0.24*clamp(L-8000,0,8000) + 0.17*clamp(L-16000,0,16000) + 0.12*clamp(L-32000,0,32000) + 0.06*max(L-64000,0). S2 hybrid ($0.31/flight list): 1k flights L=$310 -> billed $310 (above Standard $100 minimum); 10k L=$3,100 -> 1000+700+539 = $2,239; 100k L=$31,000 -> 1000+700+980+1400+1920+2550 = $8,550. S1 polling ($1.445/flight list): 1k L=$1,445 -> $1,312; 10k L=$14,450 -> 1000+700+980+1400+1548 = $5,628; 100k L=$144,500 -> 1000+700+980+1400+1920+2720+3840+4830 = $17,390. Rate-limit check: 100k flights x 38 AeroAPI events / 30 days = 127k/day = 1.47/s average; with a 4-5x peak factor (departure banks) that is 6-7 result sets/s, above Standard's 5/s, so 100k scale needs Premium ($1,000 minimum, 100/s, already below projected spend) or a token-bucket smoother in front of the provider client. 10k: 12.7k/day = 0.15/s average, Standard is fine.

findings.topic: Cloudflare Workers Paid pricing (verified)
findings.detail: Base $5/month. Requests: 10M included, then $0.30/M. CPU time: 30M CPU-ms included, then $0.02/M CPU-ms. Limits: 30 s CPU default (configurable to 5 min), 128 MB memory, 10,000 subrequests/request; Cron Trigger CPU 30 s (<1h interval) or 15 min (>=1h). Workers Logs: 20M events included, $0.60/M after, 7-day retention. Hyperdrive: included in Free and Paid, unlimited queries on Paid, no per-query fee, cache included. Whether cron invocations are counted as billable requests was not stated on the cron page (unverified; assume yes, it is immaterial: <10k/month).

findings.topic: Cloudflare Durable Objects pricing and lifecycle (verified)
findings.detail: Requests: 1M/month included, then $0.15/M; counts HTTP requests, RPC sessions, WebSocket messages (20:1 incoming ratio) and alarm invocations. Duration: 400,000 GB-s included, then $12.50/M GB-s; billed as wall-clock at 128 MB allocation while the object is active and not eligible for hibernation. SQLite: rows read 25B included then $0.001/M; rows written 50M included then $1.00/M; storage 5 GB-month included then $0.20/GB-month; each setAlarm() is billed as one row written. Lifecycle: a hibernateable object (no non-hibernatable work pending) hibernates after 10 s idle and idle time is not billed; a non-hibernateable object stays in memory 70-140 s and IS billed while idle. Limits: unlimited objects, 10 GB storage per object, soft limit 1,000 requests/s per object, one alarm per object at a time (multiplex your own schedule inside one alarm). Alarms are at-least-once with exponential backoff from 2 s up to 6 retries. Design implication: the FlightTracker DO must not hold open WebSockets or long-lived timers so it hibernates between alarms; then duration per flight is just the sum of alarm handler wall-clock (dominated by provider HTTP latency).

findings.topic: ADS-B community position providers: rate limits and terms (verified, material risk)
findings.detail: adsb.fi: 'public endpoints are rate limited to 1 request per second'; endpoints /v2/hex/[hex], /v2/callsign/[callsign], /v2/registration/[reg]; terms: 'for personal, non-commercial use only', 'contact us if you have commercial or higher request rate requirements'. adsb.lol: 'Rate limits are dynamic based on the environment load'; 'In the future, you will require an API key which you can obtain by feeding adsb.lol'; data licensed ODbL 1.0, 'available to everyone'. airplanes.live: responses conform to the ADSBExchange v2 API; callsign endpoint accepts multiple callsigns (request limited to 1000 or 8000 characters); 'provided for educational and non-commercial purposes only'. Capacity math: at 100k flights/month = 3,333/day x 3h = 417 airborne on average, ~1,000 at peak; per-aircraft polling at 30 s = 33 req/s peak, 60 s = 17 req/s, i.e. 17-33x over a 1 req/s limit. Batched multi-hex requests (~140 hexes per 1,000-char request) reduce this to ~8 requests per 30 s = 0.27 req/s. Conclusion: positions must be polled by ONE PositionPoller DO (or a few shards) issuing batched hex queries, never per-FlightTracker; and because two of three providers forbid commercial use, a paid position feed (AeroAPI position $0.010/result set, FR24, or FlightAware Firehose) is an open decision before 10k flights/month.

findings.topic: Scale assumptions used for infra model
findings.detail: F = monthly unique tracked flights: 1k / 10k / 100k. Sharing ratio r (subscribers per flight): 1.2 / 1.5 / 2.5 (provider cost is independent of r by architecture; r only drives user-side load). Flights per active user per month: 2.0. MAU U = F*r/2 = 600 / 7,500 / 125,000. Mobile API calls: 50/user/day -> 0.9M / 11.25M / 187.5M Worker requests/month. Worker CPU: 5 ms/request average (Hono + Hyperdrive query). Share of API calls hitting a DO: 30% (flight detail reads); hitting KV: 20% (METAR/boards). DO work per flight (S2 hybrid): 42 status alarms + 8 alert webhooks + 360 position RPCs from PositionPoller = 410 DO requests; wall-clock 0.4 s per status alarm, 0.2 s per position write, 0.1 s per webhook, 0.05 s per read -> ~90 s active -> 11.3 GB-s/flight; ~1,000 SQLite rows written/flight (state + timeline + setAlarm per event). Queue messages: 10 status events x r subscribers per flight + 20 email-parse messages per email-sync user (30% of users) per month; 3 ops per message. Neon: always-on compute 0.25 / 0.5 / 2.0 CU average, storage 2 / 10 / 60 GB. Pro conversion 3% at $4.99/month for RevenueCat MTR. Email sends 0.5/user/month. Workers Logs sampled at 10% at 100k.

findings.topic: Monthly cost table at 100k tracked flights (S2 hybrid)
findings.detail: AeroAPI $8,550 (list $31,000; requires Premium tier for 100 result sets/s, $1,000 minimum is already exceeded); AeroDataBox $499 (Scale, 2.4M of 4M units); Workers $5 + $53.25 requests (187.5M - 10M = 177.5M x $0.30) + $18.14 CPU (937M - 30M = 907M CPU-ms x $0.02) = $76; DO: requests 41M + 56.25M = 97.25M -> 96.25M x $0.15 = $14.44; duration 1.13M GB-s -> 730k over x $12.50/M = $9.13; rows written ~100M -> 50M over x $1.00 = $50 -> DO total ~$74; Queues 3.25M msgs x 3 = 9.75M ops -> 8.75M x $0.40 = $3.50; KV 37.5M reads -> 27.5M x $0.50 = $13.75, writes < 1M; R2 ~$1 (5k share images/month, 1 GB); Analytics Engine $0 today (would be ~230M points -> 220M x $0.25 = $55 when billing starts); Workers Logs ~$2 with 10% sampling (unsampled would be ~230M -> 210M x $0.60 = $126); Neon ~$345 (2 CU x 730 = 1,460 CU-h x $0.222 Scale = $324 + 60 GB x $0.35 = $21; Launch pricing would be $176); Sentry ~$80 (Team + ~150k overage errors x $0.0003625 = $54); EAS $375 (Production $199 + 75k MAU over x $0.005) or $19 without EAS Update; RevenueCat $187 (MTR $18,700 x 1%); Email $21 (62.5k - 3k = 59.5k x $0.35/1k). Revenue sanity check: MTR $18,700 at 3% conversion vs ~$10.2k cost gives ~45% gross margin before Apple/Google 15-30% cut; at 1.5% conversion the product loses money, so free-tier limits (e.g. max 2-3 live-tracked flights, no Live Activities) are a cost lever, not just a monetization lever.

findings.topic: Cost levers ranked by impact
findings.detail: 1) Alerts instead of 2-minute polling inside 48h: $0.905 -> $0.31 per flight list (-66%); at 100k this is $17.4k vs $8.6k billed after discounts. 2) Never poll AeroAPI before T-48h: /schedules at $0.020 x 12-27 polls = $0.24-0.54/flight vs 24 ADB units = ~$0.003-0.011. 3) 7d..48h cadence: hourly (A) is 127 polls vs 6h (B) 27 vs daily (C) 12; nothing in the data changes hourly a week out; choose C. 4) In-flight status cadence: 2 min for 3h = 90 polls; positions come from ADS-B, and AeroAPI on/in/diversion arrive as alerts, so 15 min confirmation (12 polls) loses nothing user-visible. 5) Post-arrival window: 12 polls at 10 min vs 2 targeted polls (gate-in +10 min, +2h final); use alerts 'in' event and 2 polls. 6) Position polling batched per-provider (one PositionPoller DO, multi-hex) instead of per-flight alarms: cuts DO alarm count by 360/flight (36M DO requests = $5.40 and ~72M setAlarm rows = $22 at 100k) and is the only way to fit community ADS-B rate limits. 7) Workers Logs sampling (10%): $126 -> $2 at 100k. 8) EAS Update is optional: $375 -> $19 at 100k if OTA updates are not needed. 9) Sharing ratio r does not reduce provider cost per flight (already 1 query per refresh) but raises revenue per flight; per-flight provider cost is fixed, so higher r is pure margin.

findings.topic: Budget guard numbers for the FlightTracker DO and global governor
findings.detail: Units: count every provider call as 'poll-equivalents' (PE) at list price: AeroAPI /flights/{ident} = 1 PE ($0.005); AeroAPI alert delivery = 4 PE; AeroAPI /schedules = 4 PE; AeroAPI position = 2 PE; AeroDataBox status = 0.1 PE (2 units at Scale ~ $0.00025, rounded up); ADS-B community = 0 PE but counted separately. PER-FLIGHT LIFETIME: soft cap 75 PE (~$0.375; hybrid design uses ~62 with 8 alerts), hard cap 150 PE (~$0.75) after which the flight degrades to alerts-only + 1 poll/6h and emits a metric. PER-FLIGHT PER-DAY: pre-48h phase max 2 provider calls/day (1 scheduled + 1 user-triggered, ADB only), hard 4; inside-48h/departure day: expected ~34 billable events (4 six-hourly + 5 + 15 + 2 polls + 8 alerts), soft cap 60, hard cap 120 PE/day. Per-flight AeroAPI polls: hard 0 before T-48h (routing rule, not just a cap). USER-TRIGGERED REFRESH: coalesce per flight, min 60 s between provider calls regardless of subscriber count; serve cached state otherwise; never bypass the per-flight day cap. POSITIONS: PositionPoller max 1 request/s per provider per egress, batch up to ~140 hex per request, 30 s cycle while airborne, degrade to 60 s then to AeroAPI progress_percent-only if 429/5xx rate >10% over 5 min. GLOBAL DAILY CAP (list-price dollars, AeroAPI): cap = 1.5 x (monthly list budget / 30): 1k scale $15.50/day (list $310/mo), 10k $155/day (list $3,100), 100k $1,550/day (list $31,000). Thresholds: 70% of daily cap -> alert on-call, 90% -> switch pre-48h and post-arrival refreshes to ADB-only and stretch in-flight confirmation to 30 min, 100% -> alerts-only mode (no polls except user-triggered at 1 per 10 min per flight), reset at 00:00 UTC. ADB daily unit cap: plan units/30 x 1.2 (Starter 1,600/day, Growth 16,000/day, Scale 160,000/day) with the same 70/90/100% ladder (at 100% fall back to AeroAPI /schedules for the few flights inside 3 days). RATE: AeroAPI client token bucket at 4 result sets/s on Standard (limit 5), 80/s on Premium (limit 100); ADB at 80% of plan req/s. ANOMALY: any single flight exceeding 2x its expected PE for its phase -> warning metric with flight id; >5% of flights in a day exceeding -> page. Cost attribution: every provider call writes one Analytics Engine data point with dimensions (provider, endpoint, flight_key, phase, trigger=alarm|user|webhook) and doubles (pe_cost, latency_ms), which is the 'queries per provider per day' first-class metric.

cost-model.recommendation: Adopt the hybrid provider plan: AeroDataBox (direct Starter/Growth/Scale plan, Tier-2 flight status) for all refreshes before T-48h at daily cadence; at T-48h the FlightTracker DO creates a FlightAware AeroAPI alert (filed/out/off/on/in/cancelled/diverted plus bundled delay and gate events, $0.020 per delivery) and switches to sparse AeroAPI /flights/{ident} confirmation polls (6h, then 30 min inside 3h, 15 min boarding-to-landing, 2 post-arrival), yielding ~38 billable AeroAPI events (~$0.31 list) per flight versus ~$1.15-1.45 for pure polling and ~$3.45 if the 7d..48h window were polled hourly. The technical reasons: AeroAPI /flights/{ident} cannot see more than ~2 days ahead (verified in the OpenAPI spec), so pre-48h AeroAPI refreshes would have to use /schedules at 4x the price; an alert delivery costs exactly 4 status polls, so alerts win whenever the polling interval would be under ~4x the natural event spacing, which is every window inside 48h; and volume discounts are marginal, so the per-flight cost falls from $0.31 to ~$0.085 billed at 100k flights. Positions must never be per-flight alarms: run one PositionPoller DO per provider that issues batched multi-hex queries every 30 s for all airborne flights and pushes results into FlightTracker DOs via RPC; this is the only way to stay under adsb.fi's 1 req/s and keeps DO alarm and row-write costs trivial. Keep FlightTracker hibernateable (no WebSockets in the DO; push to clients via API polling/KV or a separate fan-out) so duration billing is only handler wall-clock. Cloudflare infra is a rounding error until 100k (about $1 at 10k, ~$170 at 100k); do not spend engineering time optimizing it in Phase 0 beyond the PositionPoller split and log sampling. Trade-offs: alerts introduce webhook-delivery dependence (need a confirmation poll anyway, which is why the sparse schedule exists), AeroDataBox data quality for US gates and inbound aircraft is unverified so the pre-48h view may be thinner, and the AeroAPI Standard tier's 5 result sets/s ceiling forces Premium (100/s, $1,000 minimum, already below spend) at roughly 50k+ flights/month. Dev/CI should run on AeroAPI Personal ($5 free credit) and AeroDataBox Basic/Starter with the mocked AeroAPI adapter as the default in tests.
alternatives_rejected: AeroAPI-only polling at mandated cadence with hourly 7d..48h refreshes: $3.45/flight list ($0.905 inside 48h + 127 /schedules polls x $0.020); 127 of 308 polls buy nothing because schedule data changes at most daily a week out.

AeroAPI position endpoint for the live map: 180 polls/flight at $0.010 = $1.80/flight, 6x the entire status budget; use batched community ADS-B with graceful degradation and revisit a paid feed (FR24/Firehose) as an open decision.

Per-FlightTracker 30-second position alarms: 360 alarms + 720 SQLite rows per flight and per-aircraft ADS-B requests at 17-33 req/s peak at 100k, violating provider rate limits; replaced by one batched PositionPoller DO.
Hourly status polling between 7 days and 48 hours on AeroDataBox as a compromise: 120 x 2 units = 240 units/flight vs 24 for daily, 10x the ADB cost for no user-visible benefit.

AeroDataBox-only in production: cheapest ($0.05-0.10/flight) and its 2026 webhook Flight Alert API (1 credit per flight-item notification) is attractive, but no verified US gate/baggage/inbound-aircraft quality, 20 req/s ceiling on Scale is exceeded at ~50k+ flights/month, and >4M units/month is custom pricing; keep as secondary/dev and as the pre-48h source.
EAS Production plan at 10k: $199 vs Starter + MAU overage $42; Starter is cheaper until ~39k MAU (break-even where $19 + (MAU-3000) x $0.005 = $199).
Unsampled Workers Logs at 100k: ~$126/month (230M events); 10% head sampling with full capture on errors gives ~$2.
risks: ADS-B community terms: adsb.fi and airplanes.live state non-commercial use only; adsb.lol says an API key tied to feeding will be required in future. A commercial app relying on them is a ToS and availability risk; graceful degradation to 'progress bar from AeroAPI progress_percent, no map dot' must be a first-class state, and a paid position source should be decided before 10k flights/month.

AeroAPI /flights/{ident} 2-day future window (verified) means the pre-48h data path is entirely AeroDataBox; if ADB coverage of a route is poor, users see a thin flight card for 12 of 14 days. Mitigation: /schedules at $0.020 as a once-at-add fallback ($0.02/flight) when ADB returns nothing.

AeroAPI volume discounts were read as marginal bands; if they are instead applied to whole spend at the top band, 100k-scale AeroAPI spend would be lower (~$5.3k), and if they are not automatic (require contract), it would be higher; confirm with FlightAware sales before the 10k milestone.

Alert count per flight (assumed 8, 12 disrupted) is unverified; because each delivery costs 4 poll-equivalents, a 20-alert average would raise hybrid cost from $0.31 to $0.55/flight list. Instrument alerts-per-flight from day one and trim the events list (e.g. drop 'filed') if it runs hot.

AeroDataBox unit multiplier for the single-day Flight Status endpoint is unverified (assumed Tier 2 = 2 units); if it is Tier 3 = 6 units, ADB cost triples (still small: 72 units/flight, $0.009 at Scale) but the Starter plan would only cover ~550 flights/month instead of 1,600.

Rate ceilings: AeroAPI Standard 5 result sets/s is exceeded at departure-bank peaks around 50k+ flights/month; AeroDataBox Scale 20 req/s similarly. A token-bucket provider client with queue back-pressure inside the provider layer is required, not optional.

Neon compute is the largest non-provider line at 100k (~$324 on Scale); the model assumes always-on 2 CU. Heavy status-timeline writes could push this higher; keep timeline events append-only and consider moving high-churn per-flight state into the FlightTracker SQLite with periodic Postgres snapshots.
Workers Analytics Engine is currently not billed; when billing starts, one data point per provider call and API request is ~$55/month at 100k. Acceptable but should be budgeted.

Unit economics: at 3% Pro conversion and $4.99/month, 100k scale yields ~$18.7k MTR against ~$10.2k cost before app-store fees (15-30%); the free tier must cap live-tracked flights (which is where the $0.31 is spent) or the product is margin-negative below ~2.5% conversion.
open_decisions_for_owner: Approve the 7d..48h cadence downgrade from 'hourly' to daily (with ADB) and the in-flight confirmation poll at 15 min instead of 2 min when alerts are active; this is the single biggest cost decision (~3-4x on provider spend).

Confirm the AeroAPI alert event set to subscribe per flight (proposed: out, off, on, in, cancelled, diverted, plus bundled departure/arrival change events; exclude 'filed' and 'hold' initially) given $0.020 per delivery.

Decide the commercial position source path: community ADS-B (free, ToS risk, batched) for Phase 0-2, then a paid feed (AeroAPI position at $0.010/result set, FR24, or Firehose) by ~10k flights/month; or accept 'no live dot' as a Free-tier limitation.

Choose AeroDataBox purchase channel: direct Starter $19 / Growth $99 / Scale $499 (no paid overage, 5/10/20 req/s) vs RapidAPI Mega $200 with $0.0004/unit overage; direct is cheaper per unit, marketplace is easier to start.

Set free-tier limits that bound provider spend per free user (proposed: max 2 concurrently live-tracked flights, alerts-only after cap, no Live Activities), since provider cost per flight is fixed at ~$0.31 list regardless of who tracks it.

Confirm AeroAPI tier trajectory: Standard ($100 min) from launch; move to Premium ($1,000 min, 100 result sets/s, Foresight ETAs) at the point spend exceeds ~$1,000/month (~3.5k hybrid flights/month) or when peak rate exceeds 4/s.
Decide whether EAS Update (OTA) is required; it is $19 -> $375/month across scales, versus store-only releases on the Starter plan.

Approve the global daily provider spend caps and the 70/90/100% degradation ladder (1k: $15.50/day, 10k: $155/day, 100k: $1,550/day list-price AeroAPI; ADB 1.2x plan units/30) and who gets paged at 70%.
Neon plan choice: Launch ($0.106/CU-h) is sufficient through 10k; Scale ($0.222/CU-h) is only needed for >10 branches, fixed 56 CU sizes, or its compliance features; default Launch.

schema-design.summary: Verified the toolchain first: drizzle-orm `latest` is 0.45.2 with drizzle-kit 0.31.10, while 1.0.0-rc.4 sits on the `rc` tag (June 27 release, no GA), and Neon made Postgres 18 GA on 2026-05-01 and the default for new projects on 2026-06-05, which gives us native `uuidv7()` with no extension. Drizzle pg-core natively supports `check()`, `pgEnum`, partial/BRIN/GIN indexes (`.using`, `.where`), stored `generatedAlwaysAs(sql)`, `$onUpdate`, and RLS (`pgPolicy`); it has no UUIDv7 helper (use `.default(sql\`uuidv7()\`)`) and no declarative partitioning (custom SQL migrations forever if you partition). The proposed Postgres schema is ~52 tables in 16 domains, built around one `flight_instances` row per operating flight (key = operating carrier ICAO + flight number + origin-local scheduled date + origin IATA, materialised as a stored generated `flight_key` that doubles as the FlightTracker DO name), a `flight_designators` table that maps codeshare/marketing idents to the operating instance, and `flight_subscriptions` as the user-to-flight many-to-many with per-subscription prefs and soft-delete tombstones for offline sync. Hot per-flight state (positions, event outbox, budget counters, subscriber list) lives only in FlightTracker DO SQLite (10 GB/DO limit, $1/M rows written after 50M included) and is flushed to Postgres through an outbox; a ~200-point track sample is persisted at end-of-flight; positions never touch Postgres. KV holds short caches only (METAR/TAF, boards, NAS, search results, flight snapshot for read fan-out, share-page renders) and must not be used for rate limits (1 write/sec/key). R2 holds share cards, exports, import files, BTS raw files and optional full tracks, with prefix lifecycle rules. Eight decisions are flagged as irreversible or expensive: UUIDv7 ids, timestamptz-only with a separate origin-local `date`, the flight natural key, tombstone-only soft delete, denormalised `user_id` ownership without RLS in Phase 0, text+check instead of pgEnum, no partitioning plus retention jobs, and a single envelope-encryption format for secret columns. The Drizzle major version (0.45 vs 1.0-rc) is the one toolchain call the owner should make before schema code is written, since v1 changes relations, RLS syntax and the migrations folder format.

findings.topic: Toolchain facts: Drizzle versions and pg-core feature support
findings.detail: npm dist-tags: drizzle-orm latest=0.45.2, beta=1.0.0-beta.22, rc=1.0.0-rc.4; drizzle-kit latest=0.31.10. GitHub releases list v1.0.0-rc.4 (June 27, year not printed on page, sequence implies 2026) as newest; no 1.0.0 GA. v0->v1 breaking changes relevant to us: relational queries v1 removed in favour of defineRelations(); `.enableRLS()` becomes `pgTable.withRLS()`; generated columns require sql`` (already true in 0.45 usage); casing moves to `snakeCase.table()`; migrations folder v3 (no journal.json, new `name`/`applied_at` columns in migrations table). Verified pg-core APIs (0.45 docs): `uuid().defaultRandom()` (v4 only; no uuidv7 helper, use `.default(sql\`uuidv7()\`)`), `pgEnum('name',[...])`, `timestamp({ withTimezone: true, mode: 'date'|'string', precision })`, `numeric({precision,scale})`, `bigint({mode:'number'|'bigint'})`, `jsonb().$type<T>()`, `integer().generatedAlwaysAsIdentity()`, `.generatedAlwaysAs(sql|() => SQL)` STORED only (cannot reference other generated columns, no default, docs say not usable directly in PK/FK/unique constraint builders), `check('name', sql``)`, `unique().on(...)` with `.nullsNotDistinct()` (PG15+), `primaryKey({columns})`, `foreignKey({columns, foreignColumns})`, `index().on().using('btree'|'gin'|'gist'|'brin').where(sql``).concurrently()`, `.op('...')`, `$onUpdate()`, RLS via `pgRole`, `pgPolicy({as,to,for,using,withCheck})` and Neon `crudPolicy`/`authenticatedRole`. NOT supported: declarative partitioning (open issues #2854/#6235; drizzle-kit only introspects existing partitions), so partitioned tables mean hand-written SQL migrations. Hyperdrive + Drizzle: Cloudflare docs show node-postgres or postgres.js both supported, new client per request, `nodejs_compat` required; postgres.js page recommends `max: 5`, `fetch_types: false`, and `prepare: true` (Hyperdrive caches prepared statements; `prepare:false` costs extra round-trips). A community issue (cloudflare/vinext#537) reports alternating failures with lazily-evaluated Drizzle clients on Workers; mitigate by constructing the client inside the request handler.

findings.topic: Platform facts: Neon/PG18, Durable Objects SQLite, KV, R2, Queues, Analytics Engine
findings.detail: Neon: Postgres 18 GA on 2026-05-01 (preview limitations lifted), default for new projects since 2026-06-05; Neon supports PG 14-18. PG18 built-ins: `uuidv7([shift interval]) -> uuid`, `uuid_extract_timestamp(uuid) -> timestamptz`, `uuid_extract_version(uuid) -> smallint`; no pg_uuidv7 extension needed. PG18 generated columns default to VIRTUAL when unspecified (Drizzle emits STORED explicitly, so our DDL is unaffected, but hand-written SQL must say STORED). Durable Objects (SQLite-backed): 10 GB per object, 100 columns/table, 2 MB max row/blob, 100 KB max statement, 100 bound params, one alarm per object (setAlarm overrides), at-least-once alarm delivery with exponential backoff up to 6 retries (`alarmInfo.retryCount/isRetry`), `ctx.storage.sql.exec()` cursors must be consumed before the next await, `transactionSync()` for atomic multi-statement writes, PITR bookmarks 30 days, FTS5/JSON extensions available, KV API rows live in hidden `__cf_kv` table. DO pricing (Paid): rows read 25B/mo included then $0.001/M; rows written 50M/mo included then $1.00/M; storage 5 GB-mo included then $0.20/GB-mo; each setAlarm and each delete counts as a row written; index writes count. KV: key 512 B, metadata 1024 B, value 25 MiB, 1 write/sec per key (both plans), 1000 ops per invocation, min cacheTtl 30 s (min expirationTtl is 60 s: unverified (from memory)). R2: key 1,024 bytes, 5 TiB object, metadata 8,192 bytes, lifecycle rules per prefix with delete-after-days / delete-on-date / abort-multipart / IA transition, 1,000 rules per bucket. Queues: 128 KB message, 100 per batch, 100 retries, retention up to 14 days, 5,000 msg/s per queue, delaySeconds up to 24 h. Workers Analytics Engine: 20 blobs + 20 doubles per point, 16 KB blob total, 1 index (96 B), 250 points per invocation, 3-month retention (so AE is for dashboards, not system-of-record cost logs).

findings.topic: (a) Postgres schema: conventions and Drizzle idioms
findings.detail: Conventions applied to every table below. IDs: `uuid` PK with `.default(sql\`uuidv7()\`)`; rows that the API or a DO must create before the Postgres insert (offline-created subscriptions/trips, DO-generated events) get a client/Worker-generated UUIDv7 (`uuid` npm v7()). Reference tables use natural-key text PKs. Time: `timestamp({ withTimezone: true, mode: 'date' })` for every instant; local-date semantics only via `date` columns whose tz is defined by an `airports.tz` (IANA) join; DB session timezone forced to UTC. Every mutable table: `created_at timestamptz default now() not null`, `updated_at timestamptz default now() not null $onUpdate(() => new Date())`. Append-only tables have `created_at` only and no updated_at. Enumerations: `text` + `check(name, sql\`col in (...)\`)` with the TS union in packages/shared as source of truth (see decision 6). Ownership: every user-owned row has `user_id uuid references users(id) on delete cascade` even when reachable by join, and composite indexes lead with `user_id`. Soft delete: `deleted_at timestamptz` only on user-authored, sync-relevant entities; uniqueness enforced via partial unique index `where deleted_at is null`. Secrets: `bytea` ciphertext columns suffixed `_enc` plus `key_version smallint` (AES-256-GCM envelope, AAD = table:column:id). Tokens presented to clients (share links, API tokens, magic links, refresh tokens, ICS feeds) are stored only as `token_hash` (sha256 hex, `text unique`) plus a `token_prefix char(8)` for display. High-volume append tables get a BRIN index on their time column instead of B-tree. Drizzle helpers to put in packages/shared/db/columns.ts: `const id = () => uuid('id').primaryKey().default(sql\`uuidv7()\`)`, `const ts = (n: string) => timestamp(n, { withTimezone: true, mode: 'date' })`, `const timestamps = { createdAt: ts('created_at').defaultNow().notNull(), updatedAt: ts('updated_at').defaultNow().notNull().$onUpdate(() => new Date()) }`, `const enumCheck = (name, col, values) => check(name, sql\`${col} in (${sql.join(values.map(v => sql\`${v}\`), sql\`, \`)})\`)`. Partial unique: `uniqueIndex('flight_subscriptions_user_flight_uq').on(t.userId, t.flightInstanceId).where(sql\`${t.deletedAt} is null\`)`. BRIN: `index('provider_calls_requested_at_brin').using('brin', t.requestedAt)`. GIN on jsonb: `index(...).using('gin', t.extracted)`. Stored generated natural key: `flightKey: text('flight_key').generatedAlwaysAs((): SQL => sql\`${t.operatingCarrierIcao} || '-' || ${t.flightNumber} || '-' || to_char(${t.scheduledDepartureDate}, 'YYYY-MM-DD') || '-' || ${t.originIata}\`)` with `uniqueIndex('flight_instances_flight_key_uq').on(t.flightKey)` (unique index, not unique constraint, because the Drizzle docs caution against generated columns inside constraint builders; Postgres itself permits indexes on stored generated columns; verify in Phase 0 with `drizzle-kit generate`). Keep the schema in one `public` schema in Phase 0 (pgSchema namespaces add cross-schema FK friction in drizzle-kit for no benefit at this size).

findings.topic: (b) Durable Object storage schemas: FlightTracker, AirportState, UserInbox
findings.detail: FlightTracker (name = flight_key via idFromName; single writer for flight_instances; created on first subscribe). SQLite tables: `flight(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK(id=1), flight_key TEXT, flight_instance_id TEXT, phase TEXT, snapshot_json TEXT, snapshot_version INTEGER, cadence TEXT, next_refresh_at INTEGER, next_refresh_reason TEXT, last_refresh_at INTEGER, last_provider_update_at INTEGER, provider_alert_id TEXT, aeroapi_fa_flight_id TEXT, registration TEXT, icao_hex TEXT, inbound_flight_key TEXT, origin_tz TEXT, dest_tz TEXT, created_at INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER)`; `subscribers(subscription_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, user_id TEXT NOT NULL, role TEXT, muted INTEGER, overrides_json TEXT, added_at INTEGER, removed_at INTEGER)` + index(user_id) + index(removed_at); `events(seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, id TEXT UNIQUE, occurred_at INTEGER, type TEXT, field TEXT, old_json TEXT, new_json TEXT, source TEXT, provider_call_id TEXT, flushed INTEGER DEFAULT 0)` + index(flushed) (append-only; flushed rows older than 24 h pruned after flight finish); `positions(ts INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, lat REAL, lon REAL, alt_baro INTEGER, alt_geom INTEGER, gs REAL, track REAL, baro_rate INTEGER, source TEXT, seen_pos REAL, nic INTEGER)` (ring buffer; keep max 2,000 rows, ~60 s polling for a 10 h flight; pruned by ts; downsampled to <=200 points and written to flight_tracks at finish, optional full track gzipped to R2); `budget(window TEXT, provider TEXT, calls INTEGER, cost_units REAL, first_call_at INTEGER, last_call_at INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(window, provider))` where window in ('flight', 'day:YYYY-MM-DD'); per-flight cap checked before every call, per-day global cap checked against a KV-published counter written by a cron aggregator (the DO cannot see other DOs); `outbox(seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, kind TEXT, payload_json TEXT, created_at INTEGER, attempts INTEGER DEFAULT 0)` (kind in flight_event, provider_call, instance_update, notification_fanout; written in the same transactionSync as the state change; flushed to Postgres/Queues after the alarm; at-least-once alarms make this the correctness anchor); `notif_dedupe(dedupe_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, created_at INTEGER)` (alarm retry safety). Alarm: single DO alarm = min(next_refresh_at, outbox_retry_at); the cadence table (daily >7 d, hourly <48 h, 10 min <3 h, 2 min boarding..landing, stop +2 h) is computed from snapshot times each alarm; provider alerts call a `onProviderAlert()` RPC that applies the delta and re-arms the alarm immediately. Finish: at arrival+2 h write flight_tracks, flush outbox, set tracking_state=finished, then a final alarm at +24 h runs `deleteAll()` to stop storage billing (DO row writes are the cost driver: roughly 600-900 rows written per tracked flight incl. positions and index writes, ~$0.0008/flight at $1/M). AirportState (name = IATA): `meta(id=1, iata, icao, tz, last_nas_at, last_metar_at, last_taf_at)`; `delay_index(ts INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, score INTEGER, ground_stop INTEGER, gdp INTEGER, gdp_avg_delay_min INTEGER, arr_delay_min INTEGER, dep_delay_min INTEGER, closure INTEGER, reason TEXT, raw_json TEXT)` (48 h ring); `active_flights(flight_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, direction TEXT, scheduled_at INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER)` (registered by FlightTrackers; drives fan-out of airport disruption to flights and gates the refresh alarm: no active flights in the next 6 h means no alarm); `budget(window, provider)` as above. Writes METAR/TAF/NAS results to KV and periodically flushes delay_index rows to airport_delay_snapshots via a Queue. UserInbox (name = user_id): `devices(device_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, platform TEXT, tz TEXT, push_token_ids_json TEXT, last_seen_at INTEGER)`; `prefs(id=1, event_settings_json TEXT, quiet_json TEXT, plan TEXT, plan_expires_at INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER)` (pushed from Postgres on change so fan-out never reads Postgres per event); `subscription_overrides(subscription_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, overrides_json TEXT, muted INTEGER)`; `pending(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, dedupe_key TEXT UNIQUE, event_type TEXT, payload_json TEXT, deliver_after INTEGER, created_at INTEGER)` + index(deliver_after) (quiet-hours deferral and when-to-leave timers); `sent(dedupe_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, sent_at INTEGER)` (7-day ring, idempotency across Queue redelivery); `live_activities(subscription_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, device_id TEXT, update_token TEXT, state TEXT, last_content_hash TEXT)`. Flow: FlightTracker -> Queue notification-fanout (one message per subscriber batch) -> UserInbox applies prefs/quiet hours/dedupe -> APNs/FCM -> writes notifications + notification_deliveries rows via Queue to Postgres. Alarm: next deliver_after. Reasoning for a per-user DO: it turns N Postgres preference reads per flight event into zero, and gives quiet-hours timers a home without cron scans.

findings.topic: (c) KV namespace design with TTLs
findings.detail: Three namespaces: CACHE (provider-derived, safe to lose), PUBLIC (rendered public pages), CONFIG (flags, small). All values JSON with {data, fetched_at, source}. KV is eventually consistent (up to 60 s) and allows 1 write/sec per key, so it is never used for auth, entitlements, idempotency, or rate limits (use the Workers Rate Limiting binding or a DO for those: unverified (from memory) that the binding is GA on your plan). CACHE keys: `wx:metar:{ICAO}` TTL 600 s; `wx:taf:{ICAO}` TTL 1800 s; `wx:forecast:{IATA}` (Open-Meteo/NWS hourly) TTL 3600 s; `wx:nws:alerts:{IATA}` TTL 300 s; `nas:summary` TTL 120 s; `nas:airport:{IATA}` TTL 120 s; `airport:delay:{IATA}` (computed index) TTL 300 s; `board:{IATA}:{dep|arr}:{YYYYMMDDHH}` (AeroDataBox FIDS window) TTL 300 s; `search:number:{CARRIER_IATA}{NUMBER}:{YYYY-MM-DD}` TTL 900 s (provider search result before any user subscribes; dedupes the same lookup across users); `search:route:{ORIG}-{DEST}:{YYYY-MM-DD}` TTL 900 s; `flight:snapshot:{flight_key}` TTL 180 s, written by the FlightTracker on every state change (GET /flights/{key} for 500 subscribers is served from KV, not the DO; the DO is the writer only); `flight:positions:{flight_key}` TTL 120 s (last ~20 points for the map); `ref:airport:{IATA}` TTL 86400 s; `ref:airline:{ICAO}` TTL 86400 s; `ref:aircraft_type:{ICAO}` TTL 86400 s; `bts:route:{ORIG}-{DEST}` TTL 86400 s; `bts:flight:{CARRIER_IATA}{NUMBER}:{ORIG}-{DEST}` TTL 86400 s; `budget:day:{YYYY-MM-DD}:{provider}` (aggregate counter published by cron every minute from provider_call_daily/AE, read by DOs before spending) TTL 172800 s. PUBLIC keys: `share:page:{sha256(token)[0:32]}` TTL 60 s (rendered share JSON; miss -> Postgres lookup -> DO snapshot -> render); `ics:{sha256(token)[0:32]}` TTL 300 s. CONFIG keys: `cfg:flags`, `cfg:providers` (no TTL, written by admin Worker behind Cloudflare Access). Key charset restricted to [A-Z0-9:_-], all under 512 B; values well under limits. Read cost is dominated by flight:snapshot; at 100k flights/month with ~10 subscribers polling every 60 s during a 3 h window that is ~2M reads/day, which is why the snapshot is in KV and not in the DO.

findings.topic: (d) R2 key layout and lifecycle rules
findings.detail: Bucket `taxiway-public` (custom domain, cacheable, no listing): `airlines/logos/{ICAO}.svg`; `airports/hero/{IATA}.webp`; `share/cards/{YYYY}/{MM}/{share_link_id}.png` (lifecycle: delete after 30 days); `og/{flight_key}.png` (delete after 7 days); optional `tiles/{region}.pmtiles` if the map team self-hosts Protomaps via range requests. Bucket `taxiway-private` (Workers-only access): `exports/{user_id}/{job_id}.zip` (delete after 7 days; also deleted on account deletion by prefix); `imports/{user_id}/{import_id}/{original_filename}` (delete after 30 days); `tracks/{YYYY}/{MM}/{flight_key}.jsonl.gz` (full-resolution ADS-B track, optional Pro replay feature; delete after 365 days; referenced from flight_tracks.full_track_r2_key); `bts/raw/{YYYY}/{MM}/{source_zip_name}` (keep); `ml/datasets/{YYYY-MM-DD}/delay_features.parquet` (delete after 180 days); `backups/neon/{YYYY-MM-DD}.dump` if you add logical backups later. Never store email bodies, attachments, or raw provider payloads under a user prefix. Object keys stay under 1,024 bytes; per-user prefixes make GDPR purge a prefix list+delete. Lifecycle rules are prefix-scoped so each retention window above is one rule (1,000 max per bucket).

findings.topic: (e) Irreversible or expensive schema decisions with recommendations
findings.detail: 1. Primary key type: UUIDv7 (`uuid` column, `default uuidv7()` on PG18, app-generated v7 where the row is born in a Worker/DO/offline client). Why: native 16-byte type, time-ordered so B-tree inserts are append-heavy (v4's random inserts fragment indexes), generatable without coordination (offline-first mobile and DOs need client ids), and `uuid_extract_timestamp()` gives free created-ordering. ULID rejected (26-char text, no native type, 2x index size, no PG function); bigint identity rejected (requires a server round-trip to create, breaks offline create/idempotent retries, leaks row counts in URLs). Changing PK type later touches every FK. 2. Time model: timestamptz everywhere, never `timestamp without time zone`, never local wall-clock columns except `flight_instances.scheduled_departure_date` (date, origin-local) and `logbook_entries.flown_on`; tz comes from airports.tz (IANA) and is applied at read time (client and Worker use Intl/Temporal). Changing this later is a full-table rewrite plus a client contract change. 3. Flight natural key: operating carrier ICAO + flight number (digits, no leading zeros) + origin-local scheduled departure date + origin IATA, materialised as a stored generated `flight_key` that is also the DO name and the KV key segment. ICAO over IATA because IATA airline codes have controlled duplicates; date-local-at-origin because that is how airlines, BTS, and users identify a flight; origin included because the same number can serve multiple legs on one day. Provider ids (fa_flight_id) are attributes, never the key, to keep provider swap possible. The key is immutable even if the schedule slips past midnight; that case is recorded as a schedule_change event. Changing the key later means renaming every DO and rewriting designators. 4. Soft delete: tombstones (`deleted_at`) only on user-authored sync entities (flight_subscriptions, trips, logbook_entries); everything else hard-deletes via FK cascade; GDPR deletion is a hard delete of users. Tombstones are required for offline sync convergence; putting them everywhere would poison every query with `where deleted_at is null` and break FK cascade semantics. 5. Tenancy: denormalised `user_id` on every user-owned table with composite indexes led by it, enforced in a repository layer (every query builder helper takes userId). Do not enable RLS in Phase 0: Hyperdrive pools connections under one role, so per-request `set_config` must be `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction on every query path or it leaks across requests; Drizzle's `pgPolicy` exists for later defense-in-depth once query paths are stable. Adding user_id columns later means backfills on large tables. 6. Enums: `text` + `check()` with the TS union in packages/shared, not `pgEnum`. `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` cannot be used in the same transaction it was added and values cannot be dropped or reordered without type recreation, which drizzle-kit handles poorly; check constraints are drop+add (a validation scan, tolerable) and the domain set is going to churn (status vocab, event types, sources). Reserve pgEnum for nothing in Phase 0. 7. Partitioning of append tables (provider_calls, flight_events, notifications, airport_delay_snapshots): do not partition in Phase 0; use BRIN on the time column plus cron retention (90/90/90/30 days) and daily rollups. Drizzle has no declarative partitioning, so partitioning means hand-written migrations forever; at 100k flights/month the raw volume is ~6M events + ~6M provider_calls rows/month (~3.5 GB/month before retention, ~10 GB steady state), which unpartitioned Postgres with BRIN handles. Revisit at >500k flights/month. 8. Secret column format: one envelope-encryption format (`bytea`: version byte + 12-byte IV + ciphertext + 16-byte GCM tag, AAD = 'table:column:row_id', `key_version` column, master keys in Workers Secrets Store) shared by email_accounts, calendar_connections, user_identities.apple_refresh_token_enc, flight_subscriptions.confirmation_code_enc, email_extractions.confirmation_code_enc. Choosing pgcrypto or plaintext-with-TLS instead means every row is re-encrypted when you change your mind, and pgcrypto puts keys in SQL text that Neon logs can capture.
